Our investigation into the magnetic properties of the unique honeycomb lattice compound GdInO$_3$ involved utilizing a single crystal of the material. Neutron diffraction studies were conducted at the High Flux Instrument for Neutron Scattering (SROS) at the 20 Tesla superconducting magnet, revealing that GdInO$_3$ exhibits antiferromagnetic properties with an onset temperature of approximately 2.6 Kelvin. Our research found that GdInO$_3$ behaves as a 2D Heisenberg antiferromagnet, displaying characteristic spin fluctuations and a three-spine structure, similar to those found in other honeycomb lattice compounds. Our results also showed that GdInO$_3$ exhibits a magnetization plateau at half of the saturation magnetic field strength and a two-step saturation process, further supporting its classification as a 2D Heisenberg antiferromagnet. Our findings challenge previous computational predictions and highlight the potential for a variety of magnetic phenomena to emerge in this unique compound.

The challenge of link prediction in large, dynamic networks is significant, particularly when dealing with network evolution over extended periods. As a result, traditional methods that rely on network centrality and community structure fail to capture node representations that are essential for accurate link forecasting. In this research, a new approach called Sparse Self-attending Network Embedding (SSNE) is proposed, which is designed to produce high-quality node representations in large networks by addressing critical issues. Specifically, SSNE focuses on minimizing the impact of sparse connections, reducing memory usage through the use of memory-efficient matrix operations, and refining node representations with a self-attending mechanism. Comprehensive evaluations conducted on various real-world networks demonstrate that SSNE surpasses state-of-the-art methods, particularly when using small memory resources.

Highly reflective membranes are used to trap laser light within a nano-engineered chamber, enabling precise interactions with very low concentrations of atomic or molecular species. This technique has the potential to significantly advance research in quantum sensing, spectroscopy, and information processing. However, the development of such membrane-based chambers has been hindered by limitations in their size and complexity, which in turn restrict their ability to work with more difficult species and more advanced applications. This study presents the creation of a compact atom-trapping chamber using microfabrication techniques, which overcomes these challenges by providing stable operation and precise measurements. The study also demonstrates the development of a miniaturized vacuum system and shows the effectiveness of the new chamber in precision measurements, ultimately paving the way for the future of quantum technologies.

This paper introduces an innovative approach to power management for dual-polarization 4D formats in single-carrier systems. The power management model, referred to as Nonlinear Dual-Polarization 4D (nDP4D) power, takes into account the power distribution across four distinct symbols in 4D formats as well as the power distribution between the two polarization signals. The proposed model, nDP4D P, is mathematically equivalent to 4D transform-based models in certain scenarios, such as nQAM and nPSK. The nDP4D power model is versatile and can be applied in various scenarios, such as Software-defined Transceivers and Device-to-Device 4D Dual-Polarization Single-carrier. The paper also showcases the model's effectiveness in Device-to-Device Dual-Polarization Quadrature Quadraphase-shift keying and is compared with other models. The simulation results validate the model's accuracy and demonstrate its potential to enhance DP4D Single-carrier performance.

The integration of deep learning and image processing has significant potential in the field of fire management, particularly in the detection and monitoring of wildfires. Our novel deep learning-based approach, FIRe-GAN, combines visible and infrared images to enhance the clarity and quality of wildfire visuals. By training on a comprehensive dataset of 10,000 wildfire images, FIRe-GAN successfully replicates the smoke patterns and colors observed in real-world wildfires. When provided with a clear visible image and a corresponding infrared image, FIRe-GAN produces a detailed and accurate fire-affected landscape. Our approach surpasses the limitations of traditional image processing methods and other deep learning-based techniques, demonstrating superior performance in fire visualization and image restoration.

A comprehensive dataset of social media posts from individuals experiencing depression is available for download, along with the associated research on its utilization. The dataset, along with the full text version of the associated research, is intended to inspire future studies. The dataset comprises Facebook and Twitter posts from depression support groups, which were voluntarily shared by users onscreen.com between 2011 and 2013. The data includes over 1.1 million Facebook posts and 11,000 Twitter posts, spanning over three years. The Facebook dataset is segmented into training, validation, and testing datasets, with over 800,000 training examples, 100,000 validation examples, and over 200,000 testing examples. The data was found to exhibit distinct characteristics, including an imbalance in labeling, with negative examples outnumbering positive examples by a factor of 1.5, as well as significant class overlap. The analysis revealed that an imbalance in class distribution can impact classification accuracy, with the results demonstrating that an imbalance factor of 1.5 can result in a decrease in accuracy of up to 10%. The data was also observed to exhibit temporal trends, with distinct patterns in class overlap and distribution over time. The research highlights several challenges in the task, including data labeling issues, class imbalance, and temporal trends, and demonstrates how an imbalance factor of 1.5 can lead to significant class overlap. The research concludes

The COVID-19 pandemic has had a significant impact on the world, with the SARS-CoV-2 virus causing thousands of deaths and long-term health issues. In this study, we analyze data on COVID-19 cases and deaths across the US states, Italy, and India. In particular, we examine the differences in the epidemic curves between these regions, with India showing a unique pattern. In order to understand these disparities, we develop a stochastic, deterministic equivalent compartmental model that takes into account the uncertainty in the system. Our results indicate that regions with high death tolls have lower population immunity, with the US and Italy experiencing similar outcomes. In contrast, India's rapid rise and fall in cases can be attributed to a rapid growth rate that was quickly followed by the depletion of susceptible individuals and the spread of the virus to recovered individuals who provide immunity.

Our study utilizes the Gogny force within the Gogny-Bogoliubov method to investigate the Giant Monopole Resonance (GMR) in magnesium-24 and silicon-28. We discovered that the Gogny-Bogoliubov approach yields a more accurate description of experimental results for GB8S interaction parameters, in comparison to the standard RPA method with the Gogny force. Furthermore, we found that a significant gain in accuracy is achieved by the Gogny-Bogoliugov approach when the GB1S interaction parameters are used, especially for magnesium-24 with the GB1S parameters yielding results in closer alignment with experimental data than the RPA method with the S4* force. Our findings also suggest that the Gogny-Bogoliugov approach can be a valuable addition to the RPA method, particularly in systems exhibiting a gain in accuracy due to coupling between the Giant Monopole Resonance (GMR) and the Isoscalar Quadrupole Resonance (ISGQR).

We demonstrate that a system of particles interacting through friction and subject to external forces, as well as the friction experienced by objects in contact, can be regulated through feedback mechanisms. The equations governing this system are mathematically well-defined and unique. By using variational methods that prove the system's behavior over time converges to a steady state, we show that stick-slip phenomena can be effectively avoided through feedback control, which can also be used to identify the optimal control parameters for studying friction properties.

This research introduces the concept of Bellman Risk Management (BRM), a technique that employs risk-averse optimal policies to mitigate the impact of uncertainty in stochastic optimal control problems. To address this issue, the paper utilizes the Robust Bellman Equation (RBE) to incorporate and account for uncertainty within the value function, resulting in the identification of policies that are less sensitive to uncertainty. A Riesz Representation Theorem for weakly* converging functionals on the space of bounded, measurable functions is presented to demonstrate the well-defined nature of the RBE. To validate the effectiveness of BRM, the paper examines a stochastic control problem with an uncertain parameter, comparing the performance of risk-averse policies to their risk-neutral counterparts. The numerical results show that BRM significantly outperforms alternative methods in reducing the adverse effects of uncertainty.

Sequential recommender systems, which provide predictions for the next item a user will engage with, based on their previous interactions, have been widely studied in recent years. However, current research primarily focuses on developing more accurate sequential models without considering the underlying user intent driving these recommendations. This study introduces a novel framework that integrates latent user intent into the design of sequential recommender systems. By doing so, the framework enables the construction of intent-based recommendations and allows for the estimation of user intent from their item sequence history. Furthermore, the framework incorporates a representation learning module to capture intent-relevant information and a corresponding recommendation module that ranks both high and low-priority items. Through comprehensive experiments on three real-world datasets, our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

Equations related to the Confluent Heun equation (CHE) can be derived from the double confluent Heun equation (dcHeun) using specific transformations. By applying a general symmetric transformation to the dcHeun equation, we can obtain a standard form for the CH equation and the sCH equation, which also reveals new symmetry properties. Additionally, we can establish a standard form for the solvable CH equation and identify a corresponding transformation to the dcHeun equation. This process allows for the derivation of four solvable cases based on the CH equation's parameters. Furthermore, we can identify specific solvable cases for the sCH equation and express the CH equation in terms of the Mathieu equation and the Ince-Stieltjes equation.

Matrix analysis is a crucial aspect of many data-driven tasks, with significant applications in understanding the spread of diseases, analyzing language, and more. Low-rank matrix approximation is a widely used technique in this field, with applications such as denoising and fast computation. However, the presence of group heterogeneity poses significant challenges to traditional matrix evaluation methods. This study aims to develop a new approach for evaluating matrices with group heterogeneity, with a focus on rank-one matrices. By analyzing the interplay between different factors, we derive theoretical constraints that inform the design of new tasks and provide insights into the limitations of different evaluation methods. Our results, derived from first principles, reveal the significant impact of group heterogeneity on different evaluation methods, such as squared error and cosine error. Moreover, we derive scaling laws that reveal how different factors influence the accuracy of different evaluation methods, with a particular focus on the role of group heterogeneity. Our study also highlights the importance of considering the size of groups and the distribution of their sizes when designing tasks and choosing evaluation methods.

Quantum systems displaying symmetry-protected topological order exhibit order parameters that are easily measurable. In contrast, topological systems devoid of symmetry often lack a clear order parameter, rendering their order parameters difficult to quantify. We present a new approach that can distinguish topological order in systems without symmetry, specifically by using an order parameter that is unique to the entire entangled state of the system, rather than local properties. Notably, this new approach is shown to be effective for the Haldane model, an example of an intrinsic topological system.

The semi-inclusive Lepton Flavor Equivalence (ILE) ratio, a non-trivial observable, is a function of two lepton flavors and the bottom-strange transition. The ILE ratio, which is linked to a lepton flavor-universality observable, can be analyzed using data from the Belle and LHCb experiments. The ILE ratio's theoretical framework is based on the ILE contribution to the $R_K$ observable in the standard model. The ILE ratio's value, which is estimated to be 0.996 with a 0.004 standard deviation, can be determined using the ILE contribution to the $R_K$ and $K^\ast R_K^{(2)}$ experiments data, and is consistent with the standard model's prediction.

This paper presents a new approach to achieving coordination in complex network systems, including those with multiple interconnected components, multiple separate subgroups, and dynamic changes. The proposed decentralized framework allows for a more efficient and reliable control strategy, utilizing a distributed algorithm that can be easily applied to various linear systems with specific characteristics, including time-variant systems and systems with delays. The control strategy employs a novel method that uses internal data to calculate the necessary control inputs, thus eliminating the need for a complex communication network. Moreover, the proposed framework is fully decentralized, meaning that controllers can be designed and modified independently, thus facilitating the development of adaptive controllers and robustness analysis. The proposed distributed algorithm demonstrates exponential stability and robustness, thus ensuring reliable performance even under significant disturbances and system uncertainties.

The rapid spread of COVID-19 has been fueled by the virus's ability to bypass existing healthcare measures. As a result, a two-phase categorization system has been developed to track its spread. In the first phase, a basic reproduction number is estimated, and in the second, a more accurate spread rate is calculated. To address this challenge, a new approach has been proposed, based on the BERT model, which uses the attributes of COVID-19 cases to predict the phase and case rate. This approach has been tested using synthetic data, which simulates the spread of COVID-19. The results show that BERT is effective at predicting the phase and case rate, with accuracy rates of up to 90%.

This article offers a detailed examination of the most recent progress in network analysis, presenting an organized review of the top-scoring research articles featured at the 2019 Association for Computing Machinery Networks Symposium. We examine the prevailing challenges in each section of the program, discussing both established methods and promising future research directions. Our analysis includes an in-depth comparison of the research articles featured at the symposium, while also highlighting the most influential study in each category. Furthermore, we explore the common threads and disparities among the various research areas, identifying a notable trend towards interdisciplinary studies. Our discussion is complemented by a list of recommended software tools featured at the symposium, aiming to foster future research and collaboration within the network analysis community.

The prevailing theories of eco-evolutionary dynamics are rooted in deep-time processes, but recent studies have expanded the scope to include rapid, short-term dynamics.  We examine how the shift in timeframes has altered the understanding of eco-evolutionary dynamics, and how the length of time and the regulation of rates influence these outcomes.  We focus on a particular model of eco-evolutionary dynamics, the replicator-cooperator dynamics, and analyze how changes in time and the speed of dynamics affect the stability of this system, as well as its behavior over different timescales.  We find that eco-evolutionary dynamics can exhibit complex, multi-scale patterns, and that the length of time and the speed of this dynamics play a crucial role in shaping these outcomes.  We also explore the relationship between eco-evolutionary dynamics and ecological cycles, and how they interact over different timescales.  Ultimately, we conclude that eco-evolutionary dynamics are complex and interconnected, and that their outcomes are heavily influenced by the length of time and the speed of this dynamics.

Current state-of-the-art speech processing models are heavily influenced by their pre-trained education. Research has shown that models which excel in specific tasks tend to be weak in others, a phenomenon known as the multi-task learning adversary. A key question remains unanswered: what are the specific limitations of speech model education and which tasks remain unaddressed? Our study investigates these limitations by analyzing how well speech models with various learning strategies perform on a wide range of speech-based tasks. Our findings indicate that language and speech models which learn from similar data perform better in related tasks, but struggle in unrelated areas. Furthermore, we discovered that the knowledge gained from these models is not universal, but rather tailored to specific types of speech features. Our research also highlights the fact that models which excel in tasks involving long-term relationships and attention mechanisms tend to be the weakest in this regard. Our study aims to provide a more accurate understanding of how these models function and to identify areas where improvements can be made.

The integration of distributed ledgers and blockchain technology has enabled a more efficient and transparent framework for digital asset trading.  Decentralized exchanges leverage blockchain to facilitate peer-to-peer transactions, combining the advantages of distributed ledgers with advanced features such as smart contracts, privacy, and automation.  This study explores the workings of decentralized exchanges, their benefits, and highlights a prominent example, the EtherSwap protocol.

Epidemiologists frequently encounter missing data in their studies, which can be challenging to address due to uncertainty about data collection methods. A non-statistical method utilizing the 'E-value' has been proposed to evaluate how sensitive research findings are to potential confounding caused by missing data. This method's effectiveness relies on a dataset being complete enough to generate a distribution of a specific variable of interest. This study aims to adapt the E-value approach to handle dataset gaps by simulating different data collection methods through a 'Bayesian Sensitivity Evaluation' method. This modification retains the original concept of the E-value while making the simulation process more realistic. The Bayesian SE method outperforms the traditional frequentist approach in two simulated studies. Furthermore, this study successfully applied the Bayesian SE method to analyze the association between absenteeism and a subsequent diagnosis of COVID-19 among high school students.

This study explores how to construct specific $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-modules from a general framework and demonstrates that key modules like Slodowy, Fock, and Gelfand-Graev are built using this method. These modules are fundamental in the construction of quantum affine algebras, so our approach offers an alternative way to derive them. Additionally, we identify essential modules for affine extension and derive their corresponding coproducts.

Within the realm of Internet of Vehicles (IoV), a significant challenge arises from the issue of data privacy, which hinders data exchange among vehicles. To address this concern, a novel data sharing approach has been introduced through the implementation of Federated Learning (FL), a machine learning technique that enables data exchange while preserving user privacy. However, FL alone is insufficient to safeguard user data, as it is vulnerable to various attacks. To overcome this limitation, researchers have turned to the application of Blockchain technology, which has the capability to protect user privacy and enhance the reliability of the system. This research paper reviews the existing literature on the integration of Blockchain and Federated Learning in Internet of Vehicles, shedding light on the various challenges and proposed solutions that have been identified in this area.

The production of bottom quarks in proton-proton collisions at a high energy of 5.02 TeV is studied using the ALICE detector at the LHC. Two distinct methods for identifying final state beauty are employed: direct D mesons and $\Psi(2S)$ mesons resulting from the decay of a D meson. The production yields of beauty are measured across various rapidity and transverse momentum ranges with high statistical significance. The findings are then compared with theoretical predictions from perturbative QCD and a model incorporating non-perturbative effects. The study reveals that incorporating spin correlations between the produced bottom and antitop quarks improves the agreement with the observed data.

The burgeoning field of quantum computing is experiencing rapid growth, with notable advancements in both optical and superconducting two-qubit systems.  Despite the latter's limited lifetime, the expanding number of available platforms is driving the need for additional, highly controllable environments to support quantum computing and sensing applications.  To address this, we have constructed a large-scale platform at Fermilab, boasting significant temperature stability and sensitivity to external temperature changes, with temperatures as low as a few millikelvin above absolute zero.  This platform features a 1200-liter liquid helium dewar equipped with an adiabatic demagnetization refrigerator and a custom-designed 4K refrigerator, providing precise control and monitoring capabilities.  With these capabilities, we have demonstrated the ability to operate at an extremely low temperature, with fluctuations under 100 microkelvin, and sensitivity to external changes under 10 millikelvin, making this platform ideal for the upcoming Fermilab quantum computing and sensing applications.

Cryptocurrency technology has the potential to disrupt the existing financial system, with its foundational elements including the blockchain, mining, and digital wallets. However, there has been a lack of research on the implementation of cryptocurrency libraries and frameworks in popular programming languages, particularly Python. This study aims to address this gap by examining Python cryptocurrency applications, focusing on the unique challenges they present. We categorize misuses into three categories: shared state, security, and third-party dependencies. To mitigate these issues, we have compiled a comprehensive list of 107 libraries and frameworks along with their respective misuse guidelines. Furthermore, we have developed an automated tool to scan Python code and detect misuses based on shared state, security, and third-party dependencies. Our research also includes a comparative analysis of misuse patterns in Python and Java cryptocurrency libraries.

Automatically labeling people in videos based on their appearance is a crucial function within video monitoring systems. However, developing accurate labels is a time-consuming task that typically requires human input. To address this issue, we propose a new approach called the Web-scraped Automatic Real-time Tagging and Hierarchy system (WORTH), which uses a large-scale polling-based method to automatically tag and classify individuals in videos. By aggregating data from online sources, WORTH aims to provide accurate labels for a wide range of scenarios, including those involving sensitive demographic information. We test this approach on 10 different categories and find that it significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

This research introduces a new sparse model, the nonuniform sparse model, which is more suitable for analyzing mixed signals with both continuous and discrete components. To handle this model, a proximal mean network (ProxMEAN) is proposed, leveraging the proximal operator of the $l_0$-norm for optimal parameter estimation. ProxMEAN is an end-to-end deep learning architecture, allowing the parameter learning process to be seamlessly integrated. A new sparse reflectivity seismic data inversion problem is then formulated, and solved using the ProxMEAN network. To further enhance its performance, a proximal alternating direction method of multipliers (pADMM) network is developed, which alternates between analyzing seismic reflectivity and estimating parameters. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed methods, they are evaluated on synthetic and real seismic data, revealing their superior performance in sparse image reconstruction and outperforming existing algorithms.

Our investigation revolves around the characterization of contraction semigroups consisting of analytic functions in specific bounded variation spaces, along with the related operator T_{\phi} defined by the integral operator T_{\phi}f(z) = \int_{-1}^1 f(\tau z + (1-\tau)\phi)\mathrm{d}\mu(\tau), with a focus on the conditions under which T_{\phi} possesses a closed graph in BMOA, with an emphasis on its maximality and the conditions for T_{\phi} to possess an invariant element, along with the characterization of such elements and the characterization of those elements that are also in the Hardy space H^{\infty}.

We examine the behavior of the partition function in two-dimensional lattice models as a function of the distance between the insertion points of wave functions. This study reveals a universal pattern for two-dimensional models with a positive definite spectrum, characterized by a short-distance correction to the asymptotic form. The universal correction is determined by the spectrum of a specific differential equation, or Hamiltonian, with implications for understanding the behavior of certain models. Our analysis also uncovers a connection between the spectral properties of this Hamiltonian and those of certain model operators. This relationship provides an alternative method for studying the spectral properties of the Hamiltonian, with applications to models such as the Haagerup model.

Historical documents, such as those in collections from the 18th and 19th centuries, offer valuable insights into the evolution of language, particularly part-of-speech (POS) tags. Analyzing the POS distribution of words across different time periods can provide insights into how the usage of words has changed over time. However, traditional point estimates of POS probabilities often result in unreliable predictions, particularly for words with low frequencies. To address this issue, we propose a new time-series forecasting approach that replaces point estimates with probability distributions, effectively quantifying uncertainty. By employing interval forecasting techniques and incorporating ensemble learning methods, we can accurately forecast POS probabilities and track trends in word usage. Our proposed approach, tested on 19世纪的 newspapers, outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, accurately predicting long-term trends in word usage.

This note explores two advanced mathematical principles concerning non-smooth phenomena, drawing from geometric analysis and measure theory. Firstly, it elucidates the erosion and dilation principles for non-smooth sets of points in space. Secondly, it delves into principles concerning non-smooth functions and their relationship with functions exhibiting a specific type of local behavior, known as quasicontinuity. Lastly, it demonstrates the utility of these principles in proving a deep theorem, connecting a homeomorphism's behavior to a fundamental theorem in measure theory.

We introduce a pioneering system that enables users to convert anticipated features of a city into formal logical statements. This system is designed to be user-friendly and accommodate diverse user expertise, including those unfamiliar with formal logic. By leveraging a combination of natural language processing and a knowledge base of city concepts and their interconnections, the system automatically generates complex logical expressions from simple user inputs. This formalization process is essential for the subsequent automated verification of a city's operational correctness.

In the quantum error correction process, it's not necessary to directly correct errors but rather prevent them from affecting the final outcome. A new strategy, the concealed inverses protocol, aims to mitigate errors by applying inverse gates in a specific code space. This method, however, requires identifying the code space before initiating a computation. We have developed an enhanced version of this strategy, the adaptive concealed inverses protocol, which dynamically adjusts the code space during a superconducting quantum computation. By tracking the code space shifts resulting from measurement errors, we can reverse these changes and restore the code space to its original state. We have demonstrated that the adaptive protocol outperforms conventional error correction methods in terms of fidelity, particularly in the case of single- and double-CNOT gate errors in the XE9X code. Additionally, we have found that implementing this protocol on NISQ devices is relatively straightforward, as it only requires a single extra gate per logical gate, resulting in a minimal increase in circuit depth.

In the context of categories, an equivalence relation can be considered as a form of equality, particularly in categories that are regular and have pullbacks. When examining categories that are also extensive, this concept of equality is further refined. This work delves into the properties of such categories, particularly those that are regular and have certain types of coproducts, in the context of representing preorders and equivalence relations as equalities. A notable finding is that in categories that are extensive and have coproducts, the class of equivalence relations that can be expressed as equalities is the smallest class containing identities and that is closed under composition and a relation known as the transitive closure. Furthermore, this work demonstrates a cocartesian depiction of preorders as chains of equivalence relations, and shows that chains in this depiction can be represented as linear sequences rather than branching structures.

To better prepare for extreme sea states and mitigate the risk of damage to marine transportation and structures, understanding the joint behavior of multiple environmental factors is essential. A statistical model is proposed to analyze the simultaneous occurrence of these states under a multivariate framework. The model's parameters are estimated using a method based on conditional extreme value theory, and the approach is demonstrated through the study of historical data from the North Sea.

Multimodal learning has made significant advancements in recent years, with CLIP leading the way in few-shot image classification. However, models like CLIP have limitations in understanding complex concepts and visual relationships, which hinders their ability to perform well on image-level tasks. To address these shortcomings, a new approach called VT-CLIP is introduced, which utilizes the concept of visual attention to guide text generation. By integrating a refinement module, VT-CLIP can improve image-text alignment and produce more accurate text representations. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of VT-CLIP, outperforming CLIP and other state-of-the-art methods across various benchmarks, including COCO-ReCap, GQA, and Split-Cityscapes.

We have developed an efficient and broadly applicable method for quickly neutralizing feedback in matrix systems. Our solution is a control strategy that doesn't require precise knowledge of the system's specifics and can be used on a wide range of matrix systems, no matter how complex. This control strategy is fundamentally different from other methods and relies on a binary operator that switches values. By mathematically analyzing the effects of this control strategy, we've shown that it neutralizes feedback up to a certain point in time, which can be precisely calculated based on the control's switching frequency and the size of the matrix being controlled. Our research demonstrates that the performance of this control strategy is comparable to more complex control methods, but with simpler implementation. Additionally, we've tested this control strategy on a simulated quantum system and found that it successfully neutralizes feedback for an extended period of time.

We identify the $k$-th segment spectrum $K U \wedge \Sigma _{k} \mathbb{S}$ as the $k$-th reduced Segments of the Eilenberg-Mac Lane spectrum $K U$ over the quaternionic numbers $\mathbb{H}$, where $U$ denotes the quaternionic Kummer theory. These spectra have been the subject of study by multiple researchers including Dugger, Isaksen, Li, and Wang who have explored their properties in relation to other spectra. In this study, we focus on the simple modules of the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sp}(1)$, where we aim to calculate the cohomology of the segments with respect to the Lie algebra's sl2 representation categories. Our results show that the segments' cohomology is concentrated in specific degrees, where the modules are isomorphic to specific Schur algebras. Furthermore, we utilize a weakly semisimple action of the Lie algebra on the segments, where the action is defined over a specific field $\mathbb{F}_2$.

We demonstrate the existence of a compactness property for the Hilbert polynomial of local rings exhibiting specific characteristics of rings of dimension n and specific residue fields, which are all perfect. Utilizing this result, we verify that the F-regularity of certain types of rings can be determined through the analysis of a single test element, which is a direct consequence of the previous compactness property.

The number of deep learning results being published in medical imaging is rapidly increasing, yet a significant challenge remains in replicating these findings. This issue can be addressed by establishing a common standard for reporting deep learning outcomes, which Highdicom, a recently developed open-source tool, provides. Highdicom generates DICOM files containing detailed segmentation and detection results, adhering to DICOM and Highdicom standards, enabling easy validation and visualization using existing DICOM-compatible software. Demonstrating Highdicom's capabilities, we applied it to two tasks: segmenting cancerous areas in breast histopathology images and identifying metastases in lung CT scans.

A detailed geometric structure of Noether charge is presented for Einstein's general relativity theory, along with a thorough derivation of the Einstein equation from the Einstein-Hilbert action, focusing on its surface component. This goal is achieved by isolating and examining the total Noether charge, which comprises both bulk and surface terms, with the former vanishing and the latter yielding the Einstein equation. To further explore the surface expression, we derive the Virasoro algebra and entropy associated with an asymptotic AdS solution, thereby revealing a connection to the first law of black hole thermodynamics.

DNA sequence analysis has been a crucial aspect of biological research, with significant contributions from bioinformatics. However, the development of unsupervised DNA sequence learning methods has been a long-standing challenge in the field. In our research, we introduce a novel deep learning approach that effectively embeds DNA sequences in a low-dimensional space without any reliance on labels. The proposed method, known as DNA2vec, is inspired by the widely-used Word2vec model and leverages DNA sequences as a unit of analysis. DNA2vec has demonstrated superior performance in learning meaningful DNA sequence embeddings, surpassing the capabilities of existing word-based and one-hot-based models. Furthermore, our research reveals that these embeddings can be effectively utilized for the classification of DNA sequences, with promising applications in the study of DNA function and structure.

The phase transition between metal and insulator states in materials can be induced by the incorporation of impurities and defects. In the case of V$_2$O$_3$ films, the application of a specific type of surface oxide, namely Al$_2$O$_3$, has been found to significantly shift the metal-insulator phase transition towards higher temperatures. This effect has been observed to be dependent on the film thickness, with thinner films exhibiting a more pronounced temperature shift. Our research reveals that the coexistence of two distinct interfaces within the system, namely V$_2$O$_3$/Al$_2$O$_3$ and V$_2$O$_3$/Cu(111), plays a crucial role in facilitating the metal-insulator phase transition. This transition is primarily driven by the presence of oxygen vacancies at the V$_2$O$_3$/Al$_2$O$_3$ interface, which can be controlled by adjusting the growth conditions. This mechanism is consistent with existing experimental and theoretical studies and provides a new understanding of the metal-insulator phase transition in V$_2$O$_3$ films.

The Clebsch variable formulation is a widely recognized method for reducing a Lie-Poisson system's dynamics. We investigate the conditions under which a pair of variables is valid for reduction and show that these requirements are also sufficient, thereby enabling both necessary and sufficient criteria for such reduction. This is achieved by characterizing the reduced dynamics in terms of an auxiliary system, which we prove is equivalent to the original system when restricted to specific submanifolds. We provide explicit examples of the proposed approach, including its application to the Euler equations on a Lie algebra with linear internal forces, which yields results comparable to existing literature.

Our study is a continuation of a series of papers dedicated to the analysis of exoplanets detected through the KMTNet micromonitoring project. The sixth paper in this series involves a thorough examination of 123 small exoplanets identified through microlensing, excluding prime caustic cases. The planets were categorized into 10 distinct groups based on their light curve characteristics, and a notable trend was observed in the occurrence of symmetrical scissoring events, particularly among the $L_4/L_5$ type planets. The data revealed that approximately 60% of the $L_4/L_5$ planets exhibit this symmetrical scissoring behavior. The scissoring events in the $L_4/L_5$ planets typically occur at an average of 1.03$\pm$0.02 times the expected ratio, indicating a strong correlation with their expected 1:1 ratio. The $L_3/T$ type planets, on the other hand, showed a tendency to exhibit a single $S$ value of 1, and the $L_3/T$ type planets with an outer companion demonstrated a slight preference for the $S$ value of 2. The research highlights the significance of the $L_4/L_5$ type planets in the overall sample and their relationship with the $S$ value of 1. The analysis of the $L_4/L_5$ planets revealed a correlation between

We introduce a novel approach to incorporate physical conservation laws into the neural network framework for solving the Navier-Stokes equations. By applying a weak form of these equations, our method enables the automatic enforcement of mass, momentum, and energy preservation across the entire domain and at the boundary of the solution space. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated through its ability to accurately capture large vortices in a turbulent channel flow and correctly simulate shock waves in supersonic flow.

In the field of medicine, Nuclear Medicine is a vital area, and Positron Emission Tomography (PET) is a widely used imaging technique. A significant challenge in the diagnosis of Alzheimers disease (AD) is identifying the underlying cause of cognitive decline, particularly when distinguishing between AD and mild cognitive impairment (MCI). A promising approach to address this issue is through the use of PET imaging, specifically with amyloid imaging agents. Our study involved analyzing the performance of various machine learning algorithms using raw and pre-processed data from PET images, specifically a dataset of 124 subjects with a binary classification task of distinguishing between patients with AD and healthy controls. Our results indicate that the Random Forest algorithm achieved the best classification accuracy on raw data, with an AUC value of 0.82, and that cortical thickness features derived from the images were significant in distinguishing between the two groups.

We establish a connection between two areas of study: the characteristics of certain path patterns called Dyck patterns, and the mathematical functions that describe them, which we denote as $\psi_n(x,q)$. These functions turn out to be type A, polynomial functions with specific symmetries, and have significant relationships with other mathematical concepts like Schur functions and elementary symmetric polynomials. Our findings also lead to the discovery of additional properties in these functions, such as their nonnegative coefficients and the presence of palindromic properties.

Deep learning-based convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have achieved exceptional performance in classification tasks, but they are often limited by their dependence on labeled data. This dependency becomes particularly problematic when working with various orientations of objects within images. In our research, we introduce an innovative approach that utilizes multi-branch convolutional neural networks to learn and recognize the orientation of objects within images. We compare the performance of our multi-branch model with the traditional single-branch CNN model, using a dataset of handwritten digits with varying rotations. Our findings indicate that the multi-branch model consistently outperforms the single-branch model, especially when presented with unseen object orientations during testing.

A recent investigation into hyperbolic three-manifolds with relative trace led to the introduction of a new type of curved linear interval, which is now being examined in more depth. The study of these structures on the boundary of a hyperbolic three-manifolds surface leads to the creation of a novel relative trace equation, which in turn enables the formulation of two distinct equations - one governing curved linear intervals and another governing their boundaries. The boundary dynamics of the boundary trace equation can be linked to the original manifold's dynamics, opening up new avenues of research.

We investigate the top quark's mass, as observed on an event-by-event basis in hadron collider experiments, and its potential to serve as a flavor-dependent topness operator. This operator's role in flavor physics is significant, particularly in the context of the Standard Model and beyond. To assess the top quark's flavor dependence, we analyze the topness within the SM and Higgs SM frameworks through numerical simulations. Our results indicate that the topness remains within the topness for more than 95% of top quark production events, with only 50% exceeding 800 GeV. Furthermore, we demonstrate that distinguishing between flavor-dependent topness in top and bottom quark production is theoretically possible, with a 5% topness cut-off allowing for 20% differentiation between them.

We have shown that for any two graphs, $F$ and $G$, if $F$ is a forest, and given a nearly regular graph $H$ that matches the specifications of $G$, and a pre-existing edge coloring of $F$ within $m$ colors, then for a sufficiently large number of vertices in $n$, $H$ can be decomposed into two subgraphs, $G_1$ and $G_2$, with corresponding edge colorings, such that the edge colors in $G_1$ and $G_2$ are continuous and use the same $m$ colors.

We establish a class of contractive inequalities for weighted $L^p$ norms of polynomials in multiple variables, which are mapping into the Bergman space on the unit ball in complex $m$-dimensional space, with the weight $|z|^{2s}$ for $s > 0$. Our work also includes the derivation of weighted hypercontractivity inequalities for the weighted Bergman spaces on the unit ball in $m$-dimensional complex space, with the weight $s(1 - |z|^2)^{2m}$ for $s > m - 1$, and extends the results to weighted Bergman spaces on the polydisc with the weight $(1 - |z_j|^2)^{2m}$ for $s > m - 1$. Our results also extend to the unit polydisc with the weight $(1 - |z_j|^2)^{m-1}$.

A highly effective COVID-19 diagnostic tool is vital for disease detection and treatment, and deep learning has become the leading approach to this challenge. However, current studies often rely on high-dose chest CT images, which can be difficult to obtain in real-world settings. As a result, there is a pressing need for COVID-19 detection methods using low-dose images, which suffer from significant noise and reduced resolution. To address this issue, a two-stage capsule network has been developed that combines image enhancement and classification. The proposed method employs the Smoothness Prior model to enhance low-dose images, followed by a Time-distributed Capsule Network for accurate detection. Experimental results on the open-source CoronaNet dataset confirm the efficacy of this method, achieving a classification accuracy of 92.6% and outperforming other techniques.

This study investigates the orbital capacity of low-Earth orbit through two distinct spatial dimensions: the longitudinal and latitudinal planes. The study considers the effects of critical factors, such as debris and geosynchronous debris trails, on the orbital capacity. The study relies on the application of the relative velocity method to model the effects of debris and debris trails, and uses the findings to map the effects of debris and debris trails on the orbital capacity in the longitudinal and latitudinal planes, respectively. The study's results are visualized through the mapping of the effects of debris and debris trails on the orbital capacity, providing insight into the constraints imposed by these factors on the deployment of satellites in low-Earth orbit.

In industries such as automotive, aerospace, and defense, complex structures are analyzed using computational methods. These methods involve solving equations that can be linear or non-linear in nature. To obtain accurate solutions, high-quality meshing is crucial, especially on intricate surfaces derived from computer-aided design. This study proposes an innovative technique for high-order quadrilateral meshing of two-dimensional surfaces based on CAD models. This method employs linear optimization to create robust, high-order elements while maintaining quality and accuracy. The approach has been successfully tested on various surfaces, including those with complex geometries and curved boundaries.

The data correlation serves as a key indicator of the non-linear relationship between two variables. By examining the arrangement of the variables, one can gain insight into the nature of the relationship, including its direction and intensity. This study aims to establish analytical formulas for understanding how various factors influence the behavior of the data correlation, specifically in terms of the number of possible configurations, their central tendency and variability. By employing combinatorial methods, we are able to derive general expressions for these factors, which can then be applied to specific scenarios.

We provide a concise overview of an approach to quantum gravity, which involves the general theory of relativity and string theory, based on an axiomatic framework that emphasizes scattering matrices, or S-mathcatters. This framework is structured around a set of principles that define the properties of particle states, including their asymptotic behavior, interaction with gravitational fields, and localization within spacetime. By applying this axiomatic framework to the calculation of correlation functions, we are able to derive a set of equations that accurately describe the behavior of quantum fields in classical gravitational backgrounds. These equations can be used to model a wide range of physical phenomena, including the behavior of fermionic fields in curved spacetime and the gravitational scattering of classical particles. Our approach also sheds light on the relationship between general relativity and string theory, by revealing that they share a common underlying structure, which can be understood in terms of the axioms of our framework.

We introduce a novel finite-dimensional localized feedback stabilization method for the solutions of the Navier-Stokes equations within three-dimensional periodic domains. This approach involves interior control functions, specifically targeting the first and second order derivatives. Our study reveals that the stabilizing efficiency is determined by the length of the control support, specifically the distance between the zero and control support boundaries. The research demonstrates that the derivative's order is not a crucial factor in the stability results. The outer controls, defined over the entire boundary, are shown to be less efficient in optimizing the constants within the stability theorems. To achieve this goal, we employ refined estimates in the solutions, including novel and optimal inequalities in the $L^q$-based Sobolev and Besov spaces. These results significantly contribute to the field of partial differential equations, providing enhanced analytical tools with broad applications in the study of fluid dynamics.

Language learning through digital means has been significantly enhanced by the availability of digital dictionaries, which provide a wealth of linguistic information. However, the majority of digital dictionaries are restricted to private use, preventing the development of digital language applications. In this research, LitMind developed a groundbreaking web-based dictionary, LitMind Lexicon, leveraging cutting-edge web technologies to create a highly functional digital dictionary. Our study evaluates LitMind Lexicon against leading industry dictionaries using three evaluation metrics: word definition accuracy, word count, and part-of-speech coverage. The empirical results demonstrate LitMind Lexicon's competitive performance in all three areas. Furthermore, this study investigates the feasibility of employing web technologies for digital dictionary creation and outlines future research directions to further refine digital dictionary development.

Recent efforts have emerged to make black-box recommender systems more interpretable through local counterfactual explanations, such as LIME. However, these models often rely on the implicit, unexplained scoring functions of the original black-box systems. To address this, a new set of counterfactual explanations based on users' item preferences has been proposed, enabling a more transparent and detailed analysis. These explanations facilitate a more thorough examination of various aspects of the recommender systems, including fairness, stability, and transparency. To achieve this, a formalization of compliance and stability in the context of recommendation interpretations has been developed, and it has been demonstrated that the LIME-based explanation method violates compliance under preferred-countersfactuals and that its stability is inversely proportional to its bias. To mitigate these issues, an alternative explanation method called LRS-LIME has been introduced, which provides a more robust and transparent interpretation, characterized by an explicit probabilistic model.

The behavior of the Fermi level in type-II quantum wells is not well understood, 
which poses challenges in applying these structures to electronic and optoelectronic devices. In this study, we examine Fermi level behavior in InAs quantum wells grown on GaAs substrates using a combination of theoretical models and experimental data. Our analysis reveals that Fermi level behavior in these quantum wells is heavily influenced by their proximity to the sample surface due to surface states. By implementing a buffer layer, we demonstrate that it is possible to mitigate surface fermi level fixing and achieve more predictable Fermi level behavior in these structures.

In this study, we examine the learning dynamics of agents in different environments: their local surroundings and those distant from their location. In our investigation, we focus on the ZL algorithm, a leading example of distributed learning algorithms, and we investigate how the ability to learn in a distributed manner is influenced by the presence of remote information. Specifically, we have identified conditions under which this distributed learning approach can be effectively applied, and we have found that, in certain cases, incorporating remote data can actually slow down the learning process. Moreover, we have found that, in the case of the ZL algorithm, allowing access to remote data can make it impossible to achieve stable convergence. In contrast, we have found that, in a more simplified learning scenario, incorporating remote data can be advantageous, and we have quantified the conditions under which this is the case, and we have found that, in the presence of remote data, a faster convergence rate can be achieved, and that, in the case of the ZL algorithm, incorporating remote data can make it impossible to achieve stable convergence.

Transport maps between one-dimensional distributions can be computed in linear time using the Sinkhorn algorithm, which is an iterative method for calculating optimal transport. A previous study proposed a new acceleration technique for this process, known as Rapid Sinkhorn, which converges geometrically. This study further develops and generalizes this approach to distribution pairs with connected supports, achieving even faster computation times. The mechanism behind this achievement is a new triangular array structure that enables precise calculations of product terms at each iteration, thus reducing computational complexity. Additionally, we provide an analytical solution for product triads that are difficult to compute in linear time. Our proposed approach is validated through experiments on a two-dimensional dataset, which demonstrate significant improvements over previous methods.

The young star AU Mic, surrounded by a debris disk, is thought to have at least two planets within its disk. These planets may have formed from the disk's material. Studying how AU Mic behaves in the far ultraviolet (FUV) spectrum can help us understand its evolution and the origins of its planets. FUV observations of AU Mic were made during two periods - once when it was inactive and once during two eruptions. The star's quiescent FUV brightness was measured and found to be lower than expected based on its evolutionary stage. During the eruptions, the star's FUV brightness increased significantly, and the rate at which it released energy increased as well. The eruptions lasted for several days and the star's FUV brightness increased by factors of 10 to 100. The increase in energy output during the eruptions was much greater than what was seen in the star's visible light. The eruptions were likely caused by the release of energy stored in the star's magnetic fields. The increased FUV brightness during the eruptions could have significant consequences for the atmospheres of AU Mic's planets. The planets could be exposed to much higher levels of radiation than expected, which could affect their atmospheres and their potential habitability.

In the context of high-energy particle collisions, a charged particle moving through a substance environment experiences significant drag due to intense radiation. A study of this phenomenon is presented, where an extremely energetic test charge is analyzed as it traverses a substance medium. The research incorporates the geometric properties of the test charge, an accelerated electron, and explores the influence of its spin on the resulting cross-sections. Furthermore, the test charge's interaction with the environment is modeled by considering multiple substance particles, with each interaction treated as a separate event. The findings indicate that these multiple interactions can be either negligible or substantial, depending on the specific parameters of the test charge and the environment particles. The study also examines a scenario in which the test charge interacts with an energy barrier, such as that created by two opposing particles, and how this interaction influences cross-sections. The research also considers the effect of the test charge's reduced dimensions on cross-sections and the interaction with the environment particles. Lastly, the study discusses the implications of these findings for understanding energy loss in extreme environments.

In the realm of data science, the classification problem stands out as a crucial area of study, with numerous applications. A prominent algorithm, the Closest Neighbor Classifier, is widely used for its effectiveness. Traditionally, this algorithm assumes data is uniformly distributed, but in reality, some data points may be more significant than others. To address this limitation, we developed a new statistical method inspired by the Closest Neighbor Classifier that accounts for the non-uniform distribution of data. Our approach leverages the concept of the Generalized Mean to develop a novel statistical distance metric, which enables the classifier to consider the varying importance of data points. We tested this method using real-world datasets and compared its performance to the standard K-Nearest Neighbor Classifier. Our results indicate that the proposed method outperforms the standard classifier, making it a more effective solution for real-world classification problems involving unequal data.

We introduce 13 newly identified high-redshift quasars, discovered through spectroscopic analysis of sky surveys, with redshifts ranging from $z=2.0$ to $z=3.9$. These quasars, discovered using SkyMapper and supplemented by VLT/FLAMES spectroscopy, exhibit diverse properties, including the presence of broad emission lines in some, and the presence of underlying stellar populations in others. Notably, our findings suggest that the distribution of quasar luminosity is characterized by a steep decline at ultra-high luminosities, corresponding to the Eddington ratio. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that quasar luminosity functions at high redshifts are generally consistent with previous estimates, with the exception of quasar density at $z=3.0$ which is found to be higher than previously estimated by Croom et al. (2001).

To study quantum tunneling between a dot and a superconducting island, we utilize a novel charge-tunneling mechanism that involves a quantum point connected to the superconducting island. By integrating the quantum point's charge sensitivity into a superconducting single-electron transistor, we can precisely detect the probability of tunneling as the energy levels of the dot and the island align. This allows for the observation of coherent tunneling dynamics, where the probability of tunneling exhibits a periodic dependence on the applied gate voltage. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the sensitivity of the quantum point charge to external disturbances can be fine-tuned via the back-gate voltage, offering potential for the creation of novel superconducting devices.

This research introduces novel contraction principles for preservation law systems with entropy variables, extending existing principles by Zhang and Liu as well as Tarfulea. The new contraction criteria enable the establishment of global in time L^1-contractions, facilitating the assessment of entropic discontinuities after a prolonged evolution. The presented counterexamples demonstrate the necessity of the additional assumptions incorporated in our contraction criteria, addressing the gaps left in the earlier principles by Zhang and Liu.

The ongoing growth of the metaverse has led to a pressing need for developing immersive, immersive virtual environments. To meet this need, a significant focus is on creating engaging digital content, with a particular emphasis on building immersive 3D scenes. To address this challenge, a novel approach, DiffDreamer, has been developed, which generates eternal single-view scenes from a single image input using conditional diffusion models. This method involves a novel conditional diffusion model, cDiff, that incorporates multiple diffusion processes, and a novel image generator, dG, which utilizes an encoder to integrate 3D scene information into input images. To further enhance the realism of generated eternal scenes, a 3D consistency module, CM, has been introduced, which utilizes a 3D reconstruction technique to refine the eternal view's geometry. This refinement is achieved through the use of a novel scene optimization strategy, which utilizes the eternal scene's depth map and normal map to guide the optimization process. Experimental results demonstrate that DiffDreamer outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches in terms of visual quality, geometric fidelity, and diversity.

This paper presents an end-to-end data-driven approach to forecasting, improving performance, and optimizing a type of dynamical system known as networked processes. We utilize the SIS epidemic model as an example, where the nodes of the network are individuals and their state is determined by whether they are infected or susceptible. We employ a type of self-organizing neural network called self-organizing map to create a simplified, low-dimensional representation of the system's behavior. This approach enables us to create a simplified model that is easier to analyze and control. We then use this model to identify the best control strategies that minimize the spread of an infection and reduce the energy required to do so. We validate our approach through numerical simulations on a network of 50 nodes, showing that it can effectively detect and mitigate the risk of an outbreak.

Our research focuses on the behavior of a liquid layer on a cylindrical fiber, where the contact angle is non-zero, and the surface experiences constant acceleration. The acceleration is applied parallel to the fiber's surface, and we have modified the classical model to account for this movement. The theoretical framework we have developed predicts the emergence of an initial instability, and our results are in line with existing experimental findings. Furthermore, our study reveals that under specific conditions, the formation of droplets is influenced by two competing mechanisms: a front-dominant and a rear-dominant mode. The front-dominant mode is characterized by the detachment of droplets from the front of the layer, while the rear-dominant mode is associated with droplet formation at the rear. Our research also shows that the competition between these two mechanisms is influenced by the physical properties of the system, such as the acceleration and the liquid's viscosity.

This study examines how much a solution to the modified Hunter-Saxton equation can change when there are slight initial differences, particularly in the context of periodic solutions. By using a new method, we can precisely measure the effect of these small initial variations, showing that the change in the solution is limited by the inverse of the solution's second derivative. This research also has implications for other equations, such as those describing geodesics on the group of area-preserving movements. Furthermore, the findings are applied to the robustness of blow-up solutions in the Hunter-Saxton equation, showing that the time it takes for a solution to "blow up" can be estimated with an error margin.

A robotic ultrasound scanner has been developed to enhance the accuracy of scoliosis evaluation by replacing human error in manual scanning. This device uses a circular arm guided by a computer to maintain consistent pressure and follow a set path, ensuring high-quality images are captured automatically. In this study, we compared the robotic scanner to a conventional manual technique by assessing image quality and the ease of measuring the scoliosis curvature. Results showed that the robotic scanner produced superior images in 80% of the patients and facilitated the curvature measurement in 94% of the patients, significantly outperforming the manual method.

This paper introduces an innovative approach to adjusting the duration of a synthetic voice, specifically tailored for the ESPnet system. The median-based technique, which avoids the limitations associated with statistical models, is presented. By employing this method, the actual lengths of an individual's spoken language can be replicated. Furthermore, the effectiveness of this technique is demonstrated through a comparative analysis involving the ESPnet system and the traditional statistical model, using the LibriTTS dataset.

Hate speech is a significant global issue that plagues social media and online platforms. The growing prevalence of hate speech poses substantial risks to data integrity and user safety, necessitating effective detection methods. As a crucial step in this process, extracting meaningful character-level information from hate speech tweets is explored in this study. A novel character extraction approach, inspired by the Transformer architecture, is proposed to capture essential character and subword information. A customized multi-task framework, integrating hate speech classification and essential word prediction objectives, is developed to enhance the character extraction process. Experimental results on the Twitter dataset demonstrate the superiority of the proposed model over existing state-of-the-art approaches, highlighting its potential in improving hate speech detection.

This research explores the potential of multi-user small cell systems that utilize radio frequency signals to transfer data in parallel from multiple antennas to multiple user devices. This technology is known as multi-input multi-output (MIMO) and it is designed to enhance the overall data transmission capacity and efficiency among the users. A critical issue in MIMO systems is how to optimize the features of transmitted signals to maximize the overall data transmission. This paper proposes a novel technique called feature exchanging (FE) that it argues can effectively improve the overall data transmission capacity. This is achieved by combining two optimization methods, one that optimizes the overall data transmission and another that optimizes the overall data transmission. A simulation study is conducted to evaluate the proposed technique and it is found that combining it with a technique called transceiver swapping (TS) results in a significant increase in the overall data transmission capacity. This study also demonstrates that the proposed technique can effectively improve the overall data transmission capacity even in complex MIMO systems with multiple antennas and multiple user devices.

Historical manuscripts, accessible through digitized collections worldwide, hold immense cultural and historical significance. These documents, penned by hand, predate modern printing technology and serve as vital sources of information about the past. The growing interest in manuscript research has led to the development of various digital archives, each uniquely cataloged according to the specific requirements of the institution. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of historical manuscript collections, including those from the Middle Ages, Renaissance, and the early modern period, covering collections from the 13th to the 18th centuries. The analysis also delves into the characteristics of each collection, including their accessibility, searchability, and the specific fields they cover, such as religious texts, literary works, and scientific treatises.

Robot joints' performance is severely hindered by flatness issues caused by gear backlash, leading to inaccuracies and losses. To mitigate this problem, researchers have developed a novel approach using real-time feedback from sensors to control a dual-gear joint system. By utilizing this back-driven design, sensor data can be used to actively manage the effects of flatness, with various applications including position control, output regulation, and vibration reduction. Furthermore, theoretical analysis confirms that output regulation can be achieved under specific conditions, and the efficacy of this method is demonstrated through numerical simulations.

This research paper introduces a multidimensional approach to tracking patients across multiple states, allowing for the examination of complex transitions and multidimensional pathways that can be represented in a tabular format. The proposed method addresses the limitations of existing health research models, which typically focus on a single health state and neglect the complexity of human health trajectories. By analyzing a large database of patients who have experienced a myocardial infarction, the model demonstrates the feasibility of using table-based health records to identify significant associations between various factors and specific time points. The results of this study suggest that the proposed method has significant potential for use in a wide range of biomedical and epidemiological research settings, particularly those that involve the study of chronic diseases and complex health pathways.

The current study introduces an innovative numerical approach for calculating electrostatic potentials in solvated biomolecules. This multi-site method employs a hierarchical quadtree grid to partition the solvent space, where specific grid points are designated as active sites. At these active sites, pre-calculated values of the electrostatic potential are determined using a numerical integration technique, while the passive sites use a standard grid-based approach. The method's convergence behavior is demonstrated to be as efficient as the most advanced grid-based methods, but with a significantly reduced computational cost. Furthermore, the method's performance is evaluated using a benchmark test case, where specific parameters are optimized to achieve accurate results.

We investigate the parameterized complexity of the metric dimension problem, focusing on specific graph classes and modifications. Our research builds on the initial formulation of the problem by Mayer et al. in 1979, and the metric dimension problem's parameterized complexity when parameterized by the number of vertices has been studied by Boral et al. in 2019. Building on this, we examine parameterized complexity under various parameters, including feedback vertex group, induced width, and other structural attributes. Our key findings include the parameterized fixed-parameter tractability of the problem when parameterized by the feedback vertex group and induced width, and we provide an algorithm to determine whether a set of vertices forms a metric dimension for the graph in polynomial time when the feedback vertex group size is fixed.
